{
  "primary_meaning": "To set apart as holy unto God or to make holy (ceremonially, positionally, or progressively) by divine action, especially the Holy Spirit's work conforming believers to Christ",
  "primary_basis": [
    "John 17:17-19",
    "1 Thessalonians 4:3-7",
    "Hebrews 10:10-14",
    "1 Corinthians 1:2 and 6:11",
    "Leviticus 20:7-8 and 22:32",
    "1 Peter 1:2 and 15-16",
    "Ephesians 5:25-27"
  ],
  "alternatives": [
    {
      "meaning": "Positional or definitive sanctification: believers are declared holy and set apart once-for-all at conversion through union with Christ",
      "basis": [
        "Hebrews 10:10",
        "1 Corinthians 1:2",
        "1 Corinthians 6:11",
        "Acts 26:18"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Progressive or experiential sanctification: the ongoing lifelong process of moral and spiritual growth in holiness",
      "basis": [
        "1 Thessalonians 4:3",
        "2 Corinthians 7:1",
        "Romans 6:19-22",
        "Philippians 2:12-13"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Entire or instantaneous sanctification as a second definite work of grace (perfect love or eradication of the sinful nature in this life)",
      "basis": [
        "1 Thessalonians 5:23",
        "Hebrews 12:14",
        "Matthew 5:48",
        "1 John 1:7-9 (as interpreted in Holiness tradition)"
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Ritual or ceremonial consecration of objects, places, or persons for sacred use (primarily Old Testament cultic sense)",
      "basis": [
        "Exodus 29:36-37",
        "Exodus 40:9-13",
        "Leviticus 8:10-12",
        "2 Chronicles 29:5"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    }
  ],
  "has_settled_consensus": true,
  "confidence": "high",
  "notes": "Core lexical and theological sense of 'make/set apart as holy' is nearly universal across Christian traditions and biblical scholarship; variation concerns timing, extent, and relation to justification rather than the basic meaning itself."
}
